danish.title: Syvende bog (1810–11) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Bibelens legende fortæller os, at fraværet af arbejde — lediggang — var en betingelse for det første menneskes lyksalighed før Syndefaldet. Det faldne menneske har bevaret en kærlighed til lediggang, men forbandelsen hviler over slægten ikke blot fordi vi må søge vort brød i vort ansigts sved, men fordi vores moralske natur er sådan, at vi ikke kan være ledige og have det godt på samme tid. En indre stemme siger os, at vi tager fejl, hvis vi driver den af. Hvis mennesket kunne finde en tilstand, hvor det, skønt ledigt, følte at det opfyldte sin pligt, ville det have fundet en af betingelserne for menneskets oprindelige lyksalighed. Og en sådan tilstand af pligtmæssig og uangribelig lediggang er en hel stands lod — militærets. Militærtjenestens største tiltrækningskraft har altid bestået og vil altid bestå i denne tvungne og uangribelige lediggang.

Nikolaj Rostov oplevede denne lyksalige tilstand til fulde, da han efter 1807 fortsatte med at tjene i Pávlograd-regimentet, hvor han allerede kommanderede den eskadron, han havde overtaget fra Denisov.

Rostov var blevet en jovial, godmodig fyr, som hans moskovitiske bekendte ville have anset for dårlig stil, men som var afholdt og respekteret af kammerater, underordnede og overordnede og var vel tilfreds med sit liv. I den seneste tid, i 1809, fandt han i brevene hjemmefra stadig hyppigere klager fra sin mor over, at deres forhold blev mere og mere forvirrede, og at det var på tide, han kom hjem for at glæde og trøste sine gamle forældre.

Når han læste disse breve, følte Nikolaj en rædsel ved tanken om, at de ville trække ham bort fra de omgivelser, hvor han, beskyttet mod alle livets forviklinger, levede så roligt og stille. Han følte, at han før eller senere ville blive nødt til at vende tilbage til den hvirvel af liv med dens pinligheder og sager, der skulle bringes i orden, dens regnskaber med forvaltere, skænderier og intriger, dens bånd, selskabsliv, og med Sonjas kærlighed og hans løfte til hende. Det var alt sammen frygteligt vanskeligt og indviklet, og han svarede sin mor i kolde, formelle breve på fransk, der begyndte: »Min kære mama« og sluttede: »Deres lydige søn«, og som intet sagde om, hvornår han ville vende hjem. I 1810 fik han breve fra sine forældre, hvori de fortalte om Natáshas forlovelse med Bolkonskij, og at brylluppet ville finde sted om et år, fordi den gamle fyrste lagde hindringer i vejen. Brevet bedrøvede og krænkede Nikolaj. For det første var han ked af, at Natásha, som han holdt mere af end af nogen anden i familien, skulle gå tabt for hjemmet. For det andet beklage han fra sit husarstandpunkt, at han ikke havde været der for at vise den fyr Bolkonskij, at forbindelsen med ham ikke var nogen stor ære, og at hvis han elskede Natásha, kunne han undvære tilladelse fra sin aflægs far. Et øjeblik tøvede han, om han ikke burde søge orlov for at se Natásha, før hun blev gift, men så kom manøvrerne, og overvejelser om Sonja og om forvirringen i deres forhold, og Nikolaj udsatte det igen. Men om foråret det år modtog han et brev fra sin mor, skrevet uden faderens vidende, og det brev fik ham til at vende hjem. Hun skrev, at hvis han ikke kom og tog sig af sagerne, ville hele deres ejendom blive solgt på tvangsauktion, og de ville alle stå på bar bund. »For Guds skyld bønfalder jeg dig, kom straks, hvis du ikke vil gøre mig og hele familien ulykkelig,« skrev grevinden.
Dette brev rørte Nikolaj. Han besad den praktiske mands sunde fornuft, der viste ham, hvad han burde gøre.

Det rigtige var nu, om ikke at forlade tjenesten, så i det mindste at tage hjem på orlov. Hvorfor han skulle tage af sted, vidste han ikke; men efter sin middagslur gav han ordre til at sadle Mars, en overordentlig ondskabsfuld grå hingst, der ikke havde været redet i lang tid, og da han vendte tilbage med hesten drivvåd af sved, meddelte han Lavrúsjka (Denisovs tjener, der var forblevet hos ham) og sine kammerater, der kom om aftenen, at han søgte om orlov og tog hjem. Hvor vanskeligt og mærkeligt det end var for ham at tænke på, at han ville rejse uden at have hørt fra staben — og det interesserede ham uhyre — om han var forfremmet til kaptajn eller ville modtage Sankt Anna-ordenen for de sidste manøvrer; mærkeligt som det end var at tænke, at han ville rejse uden at have solgt sine tre røde heste til den polske grev Goluchovski, der bød på hestene, som Rostov havde veddet på, at han ville sælge for to tusind rubler; ufatteligt som det end forekom, at ballet, som husarerne gav til ære for den polske frøken Przazdziecka (i kappestrid med ulanerne, der havde givet et til ære for deres polske frøken Borzozowska), ville finde sted uden ham — vidste han, at han måtte tage bort fra denne gode, lyse verden til et sted, hvor alt var dumt og forvirret. En uge senere fik han sin orlov. Hans husarkammerater — ikke blot fra hans eget regiment, men fra hele brigaden — gav Rostov en middag, hvortil man betalte femten rubler per kuvert, og hvor der var to orkestre og to sangkor. Rostov dansede trepak med major Básov; de berusede officerer kastede Rostov i luften, omfavnede ham og tabte ham; soldaterne fra tredje eskadron kastede ham også i luften og råbte hurra! Så satte de ham i hans slæde og fulgte ham til den første poststation.

Under den første halvdel af rejsen — fra Krementjúg til Kiev — gik alle Rostovs tanker, som sædvanligt i sådanne tilfælde, bagud til eskadronen. Men da han var kommet over halvvejs, begyndte han at glemme sine tre røde heste og Dozjojvéjko, sin kvartermester, og spekulerede ængsteligt på, hvordan det ville være i Otrádnoe, og hvad han ville finde der. Tankerne om hjemmet blev stærkere, jo nærmere han kom — langt stærkere, som om denne følelse var underlagt den lov, ifølge hvilken tiltrækningen er omvendt proportional med kvadratet på afstanden. Ved den sidste poststation før Otrádnoe gav han kusken tre rublers drikkepenge, og da han ankom, løb han åndeløst, som en dreng, op ad trappen til sit hjem.

Efter henrykkelsen ved gensynet og den mærkelige følelse af utilfredsstillet forventning — følelsen af »alt er jo det samme, hvorfor havde jeg så travlt?« — begyndte Nikolaj at falde til ro i sin gamle hjemlige verden. Hans far og mor var stort set de samme, blot lidt ældre. Det nye hos dem var en vis uro og lejlighedsvis uenighed, som der ikke havde været før, og som, fandt Nikolaj snart ud af, skyldtes den dårlige tilstand af deres økonomi. Sonja var næsten tyve; hun var holdt op med at blive kønnere og lovede ikke mere, end hun allerede var, men det var nok. Hun udstrålede lykke og kærlighed fra det øjeblik, Nikolaj vendte hjem, og denne trofaste, uforanderlige kærlighed fra denne pige virkede oplivende på ham. Petja og Natásha overraskede Nikolaj mest. Petja var en stor, flot dreng på tretten, munter, vittig og uartig, med en stemme, der allerede var ved at gå i overgang. Hvad angik Natásha, undrede og morede Nikolaj sig længe, hver gang han så på hende.
»Du er slet ikke den samme,« sagde han.
»Hvordan? Er jeg blevet grimmere?«
»Tværtimod, men hvilken værdighed! En fyrstinde!« hviskede han til hende.
»Ja, ja, ja!« råbte Natásha glad.
Hun fortalte ham om sin kærlighed til fyrst Andrej og om hans besøg i Otrádnoe og viste ham hans seneste brev.
»Nå, er du glad?« spurgte Natásha. »Jeg er så rolig og lykkelig nu.«
»Meget glad,« svarede Nikolaj. »Han er en udmærket fyr... Og er du meget forelsket?«

»Hvordan skal jeg udtrykke det?« svarede Natásha. »Jeg var forelsket i Boris, i min lærer og i Denisov, men dette er noget helt andet. Jeg føler fred og tryghed. Jeg ved, at der ikke findes et bedre menneske end han, og jeg er rolig og tilfreds. Slet ikke som før.«

Nikolaj udtrykte sin misbilligelse af, at brylluppet var udsat et år, men Natásha angreb sin bror med harme og beviste for ham, at det ikke kunne være anderledes, og at det ville være forkert at gifte sig ind i en familie mod faderens vilje, og at hun selv ønskede det sådan.
»Du forstår det slet ikke,« sagde hun.
Nikolaj tav og gav hende ret.

Hendes bror undrede sig ofte, når han så på hende. Hun lignede slet ikke en pige, der var forelsket og adskilt fra sin forlovede. Hun var ligevægtig og rolig og lige så munter som altid. Dette forbløffede Nikolaj og fik ham endda til at betragte Bolkonskijs frieri med skepsis. Han kunne ikke tro, at hendes skæbne var beseglet, især da han ikke havde set hende sammen med fyrst Andrej. Det forekom ham altid, at der var noget, der ikke var helt rigtigt med dette planlagte ægteskab.

»Hvorfor denne udsættelse? Hvorfor ingen forlovelse?« tænkte han. En gang, da han berørte dette emne med sin mor, opdagede han til sin overraskelse og til en vis tilfredshed, at hun dybt i sin sjæl også nærede tvivl om dette ægteskab.

»Se, han skriver,« sagde hun og viste sin søn et brev fra fyrst Andrej med den skjulte harme, en mor altid har med hensyn til en datters fremtidige ægteskabelige lykke, »han skriver, at han ikke kommer før i december. Hvad kan der holde ham? Sygdom, sandsynligvis! Hans helbred er meget skrøbeligt. Sig det ikke til Natásha. Og læg ikke noget i, at hun er så munter: det er, fordi hun lever de sidste dage af sin pigetid, men jeg ved, hvordan hun er, hver gang vi modtager brev fra ham! Men Gud give, at alt går godt!« (Det sluttede hun altid med.) »Han er en udmærket mand!«

english.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Bible tells us that the absence of labor — idleness — was a condition of the first man's happiness before the Fall. Fallen man has kept a love of idleness, but the curse weighs on the race not only because we must earn our bread by the sweat of our brows, but because our moral nature is such that we cannot be both idle and at ease. An inner voice tells us we are wrong if we are idle. If a man could find a state in which he felt that though idle he was fulfilling his duty, he would have found one of the conditions of that original human happiness. And such a state of obligatory and blameless idleness is the lot of an entire class — the military. The chief attraction of military service has always been and always will be this compulsory and irreproachable idleness.

Nicholas Rostov experienced this blessed condition to the full when, after 1807, he continued to serve in the Pavlograd regiment, in which he now commanded the squadron he had taken over from Denisov.

Rostov had become a bluff, good-natured fellow whom his Moscow acquaintances would have considered a bit rough around the edges, but who was liked and respected by his comrades, subordinates, and superiors, and who was well content with his life. Of late, in 1809, he found in letters from home more and more complaints from his mother that their affairs were falling into ever-greater disorder, and that it was time for him to come back and comfort his aging parents.

Reading these letters, Nicholas felt a dread of being dragged away from the surroundings where, shielded from all of life's entanglements, he was living so calmly and quietly. He sensed that sooner or later he would have to plunge back into that whirlpool of life, with its embarrassments and problems to be sorted out, its accounts with stewards, quarrels and intrigues, its obligations, the social world, and Sonya's love and his promise to her. It was all impossibly difficult and complicated, and he replied to his mother in cold, formal letters in French, beginning "My dear Mama" and ending "Your obedient son," that said nothing about when he would return. In 1810 he received letters from his parents telling him of Natasha's engagement to Bolkonsky, and that the wedding would be in a year because the old prince was making difficulties. This letter grieved and annoyed Nicholas. First, he was sorry that Natasha — for whom he cared more than for anyone else in the family — was being lost to the home; and second, from his hussar's point of view, he regretted not having been there to show that fellow Bolkonsky that a connection with his family was no such great honor, and that if he loved Natasha he could do without his doddering father's permission. For a moment he wondered whether to apply for leave to see Natasha before her wedding, but then came the maneuvers, and his thoughts about Sonya, and the confusion of family finances — and Nicholas put it off again. But in the spring of that year he received a letter from his mother, written without his father's knowledge, and that letter persuaded him to return. She wrote that if he didn't come and take charge of things, their entire property would be sold at auction and they would all be left destitute. The count was so weak, trusted Mitenka so completely, and was so good-natured, that everyone took advantage of him and things were going from bad to worse. "For God's sake, I beg you, come at once if you don't want to make me and the whole family wretched," the countess wrote.
This letter moved Nicholas. He had the practical common sense that showed him what he ought to do.

The right thing now was, if not to resign from the service, at least to go home on leave. Why he had to go he could not exactly say; but after his afternoon nap he ordered Mars saddled — an extremely vicious gray stallion that hadn't been ridden in a long time — and when he came back with the horse lathered in sweat, he informed Lavrushka (Denisov's servant who had stayed on with him) and the comrades who turned up that evening that he was applying for leave and going home. Difficult and strange as it was to contemplate leaving without finding out from headquarters — and this interested him enormously — whether he'd been promoted to captain or would receive the Order of St. Anne for the last maneuvers; strange as it was to think of going without having sold his three roan horses to the Polish Count Golukhovski, who was haggling over the horses Rostov had bet he'd sell for two thousand rubles; incomprehensible as it was that the ball the hussars were throwing in honor of the Polish Mademoiselle Przazdziecka — in rivalry with the Uhlans, who had given one for their own Polish Mademoiselle Borzozowska — would take place without him; he knew he must leave this good, bright world for somewhere where everything was stupid and confused. A week later he got his leave. His hussar comrades — not just his regiment but the whole brigade — gave Rostov a farewell dinner at fifteen rubles a head, with two bands and two choirs of singers. Rostov danced the Trepak with Major Basov; the tipsy officers tossed, hugged, and dropped Rostov; the soldiers of the third squadron tossed him too and shouted "Hurrah!"; then they bundled him into his sleigh and escorted him to the first post station.

During the first half of the journey — from Kremenchug to Kiev — all of Rostov's thoughts, as usually happens, were still with the squadron he'd left behind. But once he was more than halfway he began to forget his three roans and his quartermaster Dozhoyveyko, and instead wondered anxiously how things would be at Otradnoe and what he would find there. His thoughts of home grew stronger the closer he got — much stronger, as if this feeling obeyed the law by which gravitational force increases as the distance decreases. At the last post station before Otradnoe he gave the driver a three-ruble tip, and on arriving he ran up the steps of his home, breathless as a boy.

After the ecstasy of reunion, and after that odd feeling of unmet expectations — the sense that "everything's the same, so why did I rush?" — Nicholas began to settle into his old home world. His father and mother were much the same, only a little older. What was new about them was a certain anxiety and occasional discord that hadn't existed before, and which, as Nicholas soon discovered, was caused by the bad state of their finances. Sonya was nearly twenty; she had stopped growing prettier and promised nothing more than she already was, but that was enough. She radiated happiness and love from the moment Nicholas returned, and the faithful, unchanging love of this girl had a cheering effect on him. Petya and Natasha surprised Nicholas most. Petya was a big, handsome boy of thirteen — merry, witty, and mischievous, with a voice that was already breaking. As for Natasha, for a long time Nicholas just kept staring at her and laughing.
"You're not the same at all," he said.
"What? Am I uglier?"
"On the contrary — but such dignity! A princess!" he whispered to her.
"Yes, yes, yes!" cried Natasha joyfully.
She told him about her romance with Prince Andrew, about his visit to Otradnoe, and showed him his latest letter.
"Well, are you happy?" asked Natasha. "I feel so peaceful and content now."
"Very happy," answered Nicholas. "He's an excellent man... And are you very much in love?"

"How shall I put it?" replied Natasha. "I was in love with Boris, with my teacher, and with Denisov, but this is completely different. I feel calm and settled. I know that no better man exists, and I am at peace now. Not at all like before."

Nicholas expressed his disapproval of the year-long postponement of the marriage; but Natasha attacked her brother with exasperation, insisting it couldn't be otherwise, that it would be wrong to join a family against the father's wishes, and that she herself wanted it this way.
"You don't understand at all," she said.
Nicholas fell silent and agreed with her.

Her brother often wondered as he looked at her. She didn't seem at all like a girl in love and separated from her fiance. She was even-tempered, calm, and as cheerful as ever. This amazed Nicholas and even made him skeptical about Bolkonsky's courtship. He couldn't quite believe that her fate was sealed, especially since he hadn't seen her with Prince Andrew. It always seemed to him that there was something not quite right about this planned marriage.

"Why this delay? Why no formal engagement?" he thought. Once, when he touched on the subject with his mother, he discovered — to his surprise and a certain satisfaction — that deep down she too had doubts about the marriage.

"You see, he writes," she said, showing her son a letter from Prince Andrew with that hidden resentment a mother always harbors toward her daughter's future married happiness, "he writes that he won't come before December. What can be keeping him? His health, probably! It's very delicate. Don't tell Natasha. And don't think too much of her high spirits: that's because she's living through the last days of her girlhood, but I know what she's like every time a letter from him arrives! Still, God willing, everything will turn out well!" She always ended with these words. "He is an excellent man!"
